segments.text: One of the world's biggest travel platforms once had to sell cereal just to keep its startup alive.

Back in 2007, Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia had a problem: they couldn't easily afford their rent. During a busy design conference, they turned their apartment into a tiny accommodation business, using air mattresses for guests.
But turning that idea into a business was harder than they imagined. Bookings were limited, money was running out, and the founders were struggling to keep the company going.
Then, during the 2008 US election, they created something unusual: Obama O's and Cap'n McCain's. They designed collectible cereal boxes, assembled them by hand, and sold them for forty dollars each.

The unusual experiment brought in around thirty thousand dollars. It wasn't a scalable business model, but it gave Airbnb money to keep going and a story that would eventually attract the attention of investors.

That persistence helped them get into Y Combinator. But they still had to solve the real problem. They travelled to New York, met hosts, and personally improved their property photographs. They focused on making the marketplace better for real people.
Airbnb became a global travel platform. But the early lesson was already clear: when the obvious solution fails, creativity, persistence, and understanding your customers can open another door.
